patient.chief_complaint: Recurrent visual aura with headache since college, now increasing in frequency
patient.hpi:
A 24-year-old Chinese-American woman presented to the neurology clinic for evaluation of recurrent headaches with visual phenomena that started at age 19. She reports that approximately 8-10 times per year, she experiences a small blind spot in the center of her vision that gradually expands over 20-25 minutes into a bright, shimmering, crescent-shaped arc that sweeps to the periphery and then disappears. Following the resolution of the visual phenomenon, she develops a moderate-to-severe unilateral throbbing headache (typically right-sided, 7/10 intensity) with nausea and sensitivity to light, lasting 4-8 hours. She has missed several days of university and now graduate school due to these headaches.

She notes a significant increase in attack frequency since starting her PhD program 6 months ago, attributing it to stress, irregular sleep, and frequent caffeine intake (3-4 cups coffee daily). Her mother and maternal grandmother both had migraines throughout their reproductive years. She takes over-the-counter ibuprofen which gives partial relief. She has not tried triptans. She is not on oral contraceptives. She had a normal physical examination with her university health provider 4 months ago. She denies any limb weakness, numbness, speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, or any episodes that differ from her typical pattern.

family_history: Mother and maternal grandmother both had migraines (visual aura pattern); no family history of stroke or hemiplegic migraine

social_history.note: PhD candidate (computational biology); non-smoker; 3-4 cups coffee daily; social alcohol; no illicit drugs

physical_exam.general: Well-appearing young woman; headache-free at this appointment
physical_exam.neurological: Alert; oriented. Normal cranial nerves. Visual fields full by confrontation. PERRLA. No papilledema. Motor 5/5. DTR 2+ symmetric. Sensation intact. Coordination normal. Gait normal.
physical_exam.cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Migraine with typical visual aura (G43.1), ICHD-3 criteria met; episodic migraine increasing in frequency

differential.key_features: Visual seizures typically <2 min, stereotyped colored phosphenes; spreading visual aura over 20-25 min is migraine; normal EEG; family history of migraine
5-year identical history; slow spreading over 20 min; followed by headache; normal DWI; young age without vascular risk factors

optimal_actions.action: Brain MRI to exclude structural cause
Laboratory workup including inflammatory markers and antiphospholipid antibodies
Prescribe sumatriptan 100 mg for acute treatment
Address lifestyle triggers: caffeine taper, sleep schedule
Initiate preventive therapy if lifestyle modification insufficient — topiramate 25 mg titrating to 50 mg BID

critical_actions: Brain MRI to exclude structural cause
Recognize classic visual aura pattern (spreading over 20-25 minutes) as migraine
Address caffeine overuse as contributing trigger
Assess for medication overuse headache risk (ibuprofen frequency)
contraindicated_actions: Do not use ibuprofen more than 10-15 days/month (medication overuse headache risk)
Do not give triptan during visual aura phase
key_reasoning_points: Classic expanding fortification spectra over 20-25 min is pathognomonic for migraine cortical spreading depression
Strong family history (mother and grandmother) with identical pattern strongly supports genetic migraine
Increase in frequency correlates with PhD stress and high caffeine intake — modifiable factors

red_herrings.finding: High caffeine intake potentially causing secondary headaches
red_herrings.why_misleading: High caffeine can cause daily headache and analgesic overuse headache, potentially obscuring migraine diagnosis
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: 5-year history predates PhD; high caffeine increases frequency but doesn't change the underlying migraine diagnosis; address as modifiable trigger

output.report:
LITERATURE SEARCH: Caffeine and Migraine

KEY FINDINGS:
1. CAFFEINE PARADOX: Low-dose caffeine (1 cup/day) can acutely relieve migraine; high daily intake (>400mg) is a migraine trigger and increases analgesic overuse headache risk
2. CAFFEINE WITHDRAWAL: Abrupt reduction in high caffeine intake causes rebound headaches; gradual taper recommended (25% reduction per week)
3. MEDICATION OVERUSE HEADACHE: Using analgesics (including ibuprofen) >10-15 days/month can trigger chronic daily headache; assess frequency
4. RECOMMENDATION: This patient on 3-4 cups coffee daily should taper to 1 cup/day over 4 weeks; ensures consistent morning intake to avoid withdrawal
5. STRESS + SLEEP: Irregular sleep and PhD stress are known migraine triggers; sleep hygiene counseling essential

CONCLUSION: Reduce caffeine to 1 cup/day gradually; regular sleep schedule; stress management strategies.
output.summary: High caffeine intake (>400mg) is a migraine trigger; recommend gradual taper to 1 cup/day; sleep hygiene

output.report:
TREATMENT OPTIONS FOR MIGRAINE WITH AURA

ACUTE TREATMENT:
1. Sumatriptan 100 mg at headache onset — first choice (75% response rate); repeat after 2 hours if partial relief
2. Naproxen sodium 550 mg combination with sumatriptan improves outcome

PREVENTIVE THERAPY (≥4 migraine days/month):
1. Topiramate 25-100 mg/day — first-line; 50% attack reduction in RCTs; side effects: cognitive, paresthesias, weight loss
2. Propranolol 40-120 mg/day — first-line; avoid in asthma
3. Amitriptyline 10-75 mg QHS — first-line if comorbid anxiety/depression
4. Valproate — effective but avoid in women of childbearing age
5. CGRP antibodies (erenumab 70mg SC monthly) — newer, well-tolerated; approved for episodic migraine

CONCLUSION: Prescribe sumatriptan; initiate preventive with topiramate given 8-10 attacks/year increasing.
output.summary: Sumatriptan first-line acute; topiramate or propranolol preventive; CGRP monoclonal antibodies alternative

output.report:
DRUG INTERACTION REVIEW

Sumatriptan + caffeine: No significant interaction. Caffeine can enhance triptan absorption (used in Cafergot preparation). However, chronic high caffeine can cause rebound; not recommended as regular combination.

CONCLUSION: Sumatriptan safe. Reduce caffeine separately.
output.summary: No sumatriptan-caffeine interaction; address caffeine intake separately

output.impression: Normal EEG; no occipital epileptiform activity; visual aura is migraine not seizure. Clinical correlation recommended.
